articles.title: Kelly Clarkson's late ex-husband Brandon Blackstock bought a 40-acre Montana ranch after their separation; less than a year after his death, the 6,400-square-foot estate with equestrian facilities is listed for $2.9 million
articles.summary: Kelly Clarkson's late ex-husband Brandon Blackstock's sprawling Montana lodge, where he lived after their separation, has been listed for sale for $2.9
articles.body: Kelly Clarkson's late ex-husband Brandon Blackstock's sprawling Montana lodge, where he lived after their separation, has been listed for sale for $2.9 million, less than a year after his death from cancer in August 2025 at the age of 48. The 40-acre property in Butte, Montana, features a 6,400-square-foot lodge with four bedrooms, an indoor pool and spa, and an equestrian facility with an eight-stall horse barn. Blackstock purchased the property in April 2022, shortly after his divorce from Clarkson was finalised, and reportedly lived there with his partner, Brittney Marie Jones.According to Realtor.com, the sprawling property, which was listed in June, is being marketed as a premium residence that combines sophisticated architectural design with the privacy and expansive landscapes associated with Montana. The listing highlights the estate's 40 acres of land and its lodge-style home, which offers more than 6,400 square feet of living space.The property is represented by Ryan Underwood of Keller Williams Copper City Realty. Records reportedly continue to list the residence under Blackstock's full name, Narvel Brandon Blackstock.The home features four bedrooms and two-and-a-half bathrooms, along with a chef's kitchen and a spacious great room with soaring vaulted ceilings. An entire wall of windows overlooks the surrounding landscape, bringing the outdoors into the main living area. A loft sits above the great room, while the finished lower level includes additional living space and a bar area.Inside the lodge's indoor pool, spa and equestrian facilitiesOne of the property's standout features is its indoor pool and spa room, designed for year-round use. Three walls of windows surround the space, and the design allows it to be opened up to the outdoors.The primary suite is located on the main floor and is described as a secluded retreat. It includes a fireplace and an en suite bathroom equipped with a soaking tub and an integrated steam room.The estate also caters to an equestrian lifestyle, with a 3,800-square-foot horse barn featuring eight stalls, a tack room and a hay loft. Other facilities include a heated workshop, a separate car shop and three water wells.Practical features have also been incorporated to make the property accessible during Montana's harsh winters. These include snow-melt sidewalks and a paved driveway connecting directly to a county-maintained road.Brandon Blackstock moved to Montana after his divorce from Kelly ClarksonBlackstock purchased the Butte property in April 2022, one month after his divorce from Clarkson was finalised. The former couple had announced their separation in 2020 after nine years of marriage.They share two children, daughter River, now 12, and son Remington, now 10.Before their separation, Clarkson and Blackstock had relocated to Montana during the COVID-19 lockdown, embracing a quieter, more rural lifestyle with their children. The move came as the pandemic disrupted the entertainment industry, affecting Clarkson's talk show and Las Vegas residency.Following their divorce, Clarkson retained ownership of two Montana properties the couple had shared during their marriage. She later established a more permanent base in New York City in 2023, when her talk show moved from Los Angeles to the Big Apple.Blackstock, meanwhile, remained in Montana and acquired the Butte property, where he was understood to have lived with his partner, Brittney Marie Jones, who had previously worked as an assistant to Clarkson.Blackstock's love for the cowboy lifestyleBlackstock's obituary offered a glimpse into the life he built in Montana after spending more than two decades working in the music industry."After more than 20 years in the music business, Brandon found his way back to the mountains and the cowboy way of life he always wanted to live. He found a homestead and a love in Butte, Montana," the online tribute read.The tribute also spoke about his relationship with Jones and their shared business ambitions, including their efforts to establish Headwaters Livestock Auction and Valley View Rodeo."Brandon, along with his beautiful and loving partner in life and business, Brittney Marie Jones, started building a life, building companies, and working tirelessly to create Headwaters Livestock Auction and what will live on as his legacy, The Valley View Rodeo in Bozeman, Montana," the obituary stated.It further described Blackstock as someone who embraced life wholeheartedly and valued hard work and traditional cowboy culture."Brandon didn’t do anything halfway. He charged into life with both guns blazing. He was a cowboy… and valued the cowboy way of life," the tribute continued, recalling how he drove a big truck, rode a good horse and removed his hat when introducing himself.Blackstock's business ventures in MontanaBeyond real estate, Blackstock also invested in businesses that reflected his growing affinity for the Western lifestyle.In 2023, he acquired Headwaters Livestock Auction, a livestock auction business in Three Forks, Montana, which first opened in 2005. Public records reportedly indicate that he filed a petition in May 2023 seeking changes to the business licence’s name and ownership.Blackstock remains listed as the owner on the company’s website, while Jones is identified as its managing director.The two also collaborated on Valley View Rodeo, a venture established in 2023 that aims to preserve the Western way of life in a modern world.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Fernanda Louback assume secretaria no governo Ruas | G1
articles.standfirst: Vice-governadora eleita ficará à frente de uma pasta com orçamento próprio, voltada a políticas para mulheres e pessoas com deficiência em todo o estado.
articles.summary: Vice-governadora eleita ficará à frente de uma pasta com orçamento próprio, voltada a políticas para mulheres e pessoas com deficiência em todo o estado.
articles.body:
Douglas Ruas anuncia Fernanda Louback como primeira secretária do novo governo do RJ — Foto: Divulgação

O governador eleito do Rio de Janeiro , Douglas Ruas (PL), anunciou nesta terça-feira (13) o primeiro nome de seu secretariado. A vice-governadora eleita Fernanda Louback ficará à frente da Secretaria de Estado da Inclusão e da Mulher.

Empreendedora e mãe de duas meninas autistas, Fernanda é vereadora de Niterói e tem atuação voltada à defesa dos direitos das pessoas com deficiência e das famílias atípicas.

Segundo o governo eleito, a nova pasta terá orçamento próprio e deverá ampliar a integração de políticas de inclusão e de direitos das mulheres entre as diferentes áreas da administração estadual.

Em declaração divulgada no anúncio, Fernanda afirmou que pretende ampliar as políticas públicas voltadas a esses grupos.

“Conheço os desafios enfrentados pelas famílias que precisam de acolhimento, acesso a serviços e oportunidades. Minha trajetória na vida pública sempre foi pautada pela defesa da inclusão e dos direitos das pessoas com deficiência".

"Agora, teremos a oportunidade de ampliar esse trabalho, fortalecendo as políticas públicas para mulheres e pessoas com deficiência em todo o estado. Queremos construir um governo que acolha, escute e ofereça respostas concretas a quem mais precisa”, declarou Louback.

De acordo com o anúncio, a criação da Secretaria de Estado da Inclusão e da Mulher faz parte da estratégia de Ruas de incorporar esses temas às políticas de todas as áreas do governo, em vez de restringi-los a uma única estrutura administrativa.

O governador eleito afirmou que a pasta terá papel de articulação entre setores como saúde, educação, segurança e geração de emprego e renda.

“A secretaria terá um papel estratégico na criação dessas políticas, garantindo que essas pautas não fiquem restritas a uma única pasta, mas sejam consideradas em todas as decisões do governo. Fernanda tem experiência e conhece de perto as demandas das famílias”, disse Ruas.

Fernanda Louback tem 46 anos, é educadora física, empreendedora e vereadora de Niterói, cidade onde nasceu. Ela foi eleita para a Câmara Municipal em 2024, com cerca de 3,5 mil votos, e tem uma atuação política de perfil conservador.

Fernanda Louback é vereadora do PL por Niterói — Foto: Divulgação

Antes de entrar na política, ficou conhecida ao vencer o concurso Miss Rio de Janeiro, em 2003, quando representou Nova Friburgo. Na sequência, participou da etapa nacional da competição e, posteriormente, tornou-se empresária no ramo de joias.

Fernanda foi escolhida pelo PL para compor a chapa de Douglas Ruas depois que o ex-prefeito de Nova Iguaçu Rogério Lisboa desistiu de disputar a vice-governadoria.

A confirmação para a secretaria é o primeiro anúncio de integrante do futuro governo estadual desde que Ruas foi declarado governador eleito após a retotalização dos votos pela Justiça Eleitoral.

articles.title: Cachorra morre após ataque de cão de grande porte no Sol Nascente | G1
articles.standfirst: Ataque aconteceu no Trecho 3 do Sol Nascente. Segundo moradores, o cão já havia atacado outros animais na região.
articles.summary: Uma cachorra de 14 anos morreu no Trecho 3 do Sol Nascente após ser atacada por um cão de grande porte que já teria ferido outros animais na região.
articles.body:
Uma cachorra de 14 anos morreu após ser atacada por um cão de grande porte na manhã desta terça-feira (13), no Trecho 3 do Sol Nascente, no Distrito Federal.

Imagens gravadas por uma moradora mostram vizinhos tentando separar os animais (veja o vídeo acima).

É possível ver quando um homem bate com uma vassoura no cão.

Logo depois, outro joga um carro na direção dele.

Em seguida, um vizinho consegue puxar o animal pelo pescoço com auxílio de uma corda.

Depois de ser contido, o cão foi entregue a uma mulher, que o levou para casa

Segundo moradores, a tutora do animal não prestou socorro à cachorra atacada. Os vizinhos também afirmam que o cão já havia atacado pelo menos outros dois animais na região.

Cachorra de 14 anos morre após ser atacada por cão de grande porte no DF — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A cachorra que morreu se chamava Nayara, mas era conhecida como Nay. A vira-lata tinha 14 anos e era tutelada por Nayara Carolina Ferreira, que conversou com o g1 .

A tutora disse que quer conversar com os responsáveis pelo outro cão para entender o que aconteceu.

“Não sou contra cachorro de porte grande, inclusive já tive. E eu tinha o maior cuidado, porque sabia que, se acontecesse alguma coisa, machucaria alguém”, afirmou.

“Hoje foi a minha cachorra. E amanhã pode ser quem?”, questionou. Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não havia sido registrado nenhum boletim de ocorrrência.

articles.title: Sob chuva, apoiadores de Lula fazem ato no Largo da Batata, em SP, para mobilizar votos no 2º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Manifestação reuniu militantes, estudantes e parlamentares; presidente não participa do evento, que foi organizado para manter a mobilização da campanha nas ruas.
articles.summary: Manifestação reuniu militantes, estudantes e parlamentares; presidente não participa do evento, que foi organizado para manter a mobilização da campanha nas ruas.
articles.body:
Manifestação em apoio ao candidato à reeleição Lula (PT) no Largo da Batata, em São Paulo. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Apoiadores do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) se reuniram na noite desta terça-feira (13) no Largo da Batata, em Pinheiros, na Zona Oeste de São Paulo , para um ato de campanha em apoio à reeleição do petista. Uma estrutura com palco foi montada no local, e os manifestantes ocuparam o largo apesar da chuva no início da noite. O trânsito no entorno não foi interrompido.

Batizado de “Ato da Virada”, o evento começou por volta das 18h com militantes, muitos deles jovens e estudantes, além de parlamentares. A mobilização faz parte de uma série de atos realizados em diferentes cidades do país nesta terça-feira, segundo os organizadores.

A ideia é manter a militância mobilizada nas ruas e estimular a conquista de votos para o segundo turno, sem a expectativa de reunir uma multidão. O presidente Lula não participa do ato em São Paulo.

Entre os presentes estão os deputados estaduais petistas Eduardo Suplicy, Thainara Faria, Luiz Fernando, Paulo Fiorilo e Duda Hidalgo, além das deputadas federais Erika Hilton (PSOL) Professora Luciene Cavalcante (PSOL).

Os ex-ministros Fernando Haddad, Simone Tebet e Marina Silva também discursaram para apoiadores. O ato acabou por volta das 20h35.

O evento foi convocado pelo PT, com apoio dos partidos que integram a federação Brasil da Esperança (PCdoB e PV) e a federação PSOL-Rede. A data de realização também foi escolhida para aproveitar o dia 13, número eleitoral do PT.

A mobilização ocorre antes do segundo turno da eleição presidencial, marcado para 25 de outubro , quando Lula enfrenta o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Assim como no ato realizado no domingo (11), na Avenida Paulista, apoiadores defenderam que eleitores conversem com pessoas que não compareceram às urnas no primeiro turno , em uma tentativa de ampliar a votação do presidente.

articles.title: Papa Leão XIV foi hospitalizado com febre tifoide em 1985; momento foi decisivo em sua trajetória | G1
articles.standfirst: Pontífice, de 71 anos, foi diagnosticado nesta terça (13) com câncer de pulmão e passou por cirurgia para retirar um tumor da parte inferior do órgão.
articles.summary: Pontífice, de 71 anos, foi diagnosticado nesta terça (13) com câncer de pulmão e passou por cirurgia para retirar um tumor da parte inferior do órgão.
articles.body:
O papa Leão XIV foi diagnosticado nesta terça-feira (13) com adenocarcinoma pulmonar , um tipo de câncer no pulmão, informou o Vaticano . O pontífice passou por uma cirurgia e precisou retirar a parte inferior do pulmão direito, onde estava localizado o tumor.

Acredita-se que esta seja a segunda internação de Leão, conhecido por ser esportivo e estar em boa forma física, com partidas semanais de tênis e prática de natação. O pontífice tem 71 anos.

Quando era um jovem padre missionário, ele contraiu febre tifoide em 1985, pouco depois de chegar a Chulucanas, no Peru.

👉 A Febre Tifoide é uma doença bacteriana aguda diretamente associada a baixos níveis socioeconômicos, principalmente em regiões com condições precárias de saneamento básico. Se não tratada adequadamente, pode levar à morte.

A doença e a hospitalização foram um momento decisivo para que ele optasse por permanecer em meio à pobreza e às dificuldades do Peru, depois de ter vivido com relativo conforto em Roma .

Segundo uma entrevista concedida pelo Papa Leão a Elise Ann Allen em 2025 para a biografia “Papa Leão XIV: A Biografia” , essa decisão acabou abrindo caminho para seu pontificado.

De acordo com o livro, o pontífice contou que rezou a Deus pedindo que o deixasse morrer em vez de continuar sofrendo a dor “horrível” provocada pela febre. “Eu estava no soro e disse: ‘Se esse é o seu senso de humor, Senhor, acho que poderia fazer um pouco melhor.’”

“Obviamente, sobrevivi; me recuperei, mas acabou sendo um momento muito significativo para mim, porque foi como: ‘Bem, você já enfrentou a doença; já vê quais são as necessidades aqui. A ordem, os agostinianos, a Igreja estão dizendo: ‘Precisamos de você aqui; vá em frente.’ Nunca olhei para trás.”

Segundo a nota assinada pelo médico Luigi Carbone e pelo professor Stefano Margaritora, os exames realizados antes da cirurgia já apontavam para o diagnóstico , que foi confirmado durante a operação.

A equipe, composta por mais dois médicos, decidiu retirar o lobo inferior do pulmão de Leão por meio de técnica videoassistida.

A cirurgia durou cerca de 90 minutos, foi concluída com sucesso e não teve complicações. Leão XIV acordou normalmente e voltou ao quarto do hospital, onde se recupera.

A nota não mencionou quais serão os próximos passos do tratamento, e o Vaticano afirmou que, por enquanto, os médicos não estão falando em quimioterapia ou outras terapias, enquanto aguardam os resultados de outros exames.

A Sala de Imprensa do Vaticano destacou que o boletim médico mencionou a remoção "radical" do lobo, indicando que todo o tecido suspeito foi retirado, na expectativa de eliminar eventuais vestígios remanescentes do cânc

Os linfonodos de Leão também teriam sido retirados e examinados para determinar se o câncer havia se espalhado, mas ainda não havia informações sobre os resultados desses testes.

Segundo a agência de notícias Associated Press, médicos tiveram de aplicar uma anestesia geral e realizaram uma biópsia na lesão após a remoção.

articles.title: Location, location, Kirkland? Inside the new Costco housing trend
articles.summary: Forget good schools and curb appeal. Proximity to Costco is the hot new neighborhood amenity reshaping where Americans choose to live.
articles.body:
By any measure, Adam Staley's Costco dedication is next level . He hits his local warehouse at least four days a week for samples, deals and hot dogs . His wardrobe is proudly Kirkland Signature and he freely admits Costco is his favorite place on earth.

So when it came time for his family to hunt for a rental house in Kansas City, Missouri, Staley chose one just five blocks from his personal mecca.

"It was one of the top reasons why we wanted to choose this house," Staley said. "Walking out the door, getting in the car and being there in three minutes was a huge plus."

When house hunting, most renters and homebuyers draw up a familiar checklist: good school districts, safe neighborhoods, short commutes, enough bedrooms. But for some Americans, another priority has quietly shot to the top: Living within minutes of a Costco.

The pull of bulk paper towels, rotisserie chickens and discounted gas has created what real estate watchers call the " Costco effect " – when proximity to the wholesale giant shapes where people put down roots.

Home is where the executive membership is

On Reddit, users openly trade advice on moving closer to a Costco.

"Does anyone else only look for houses that are close enough to a Costco?" asked one user who obsessively checks Redfin maps against warehouse locations.

Another buyer relocating to Austin created a dedicated spreadsheet column with the distance to the nearest warehouse.

A third, weighing two neighborhoods in a state with only one Costco, admitted: "I'm embarrassed to say how real the consideration is for distance-to-Costco in my deliberations."

For members, proximity comes with benefits such as late-night gas runs right before closing when lines dissipate or cheap and easy weeknight dinners in the food court. In Los Angeles, developers are tapping into the trend by building hundreds of apartments directly on top of a Costco warehouse.

While living close is the dream for some , living too far creates its own frustration.

Kathy Spangler and her husband live in a Pinehurst, North Carolina, golf community more than an hour from the nearest Costco.

The retired school administrators and English teachers make a day trip out of visiting the warehouse club two or three times a year.

It was during these rare treks that Spangler coined the term "Costco envy" to describe the pang of jealousy she feels pushing two fully loaded carts past locals who popped in for a quick run.

"Whenever we're up there and I see somebody walking out with just a rotisserie chicken or rolls of toilet paper, I say I have Costco envy because they obviously live so close that they can come here and get one or two items," Spangler said.

Real estate agents say the sweet spot is typically 5 to 15 minutes away – close enough for a quick run but far enough to avoid traffic congestion and delivery truck noise.

While proximity to a warehouse rarely replaces traditional factors like school zones, it has become a powerful selling feature.

"Buyers have asked me where the closest Costco is when considering an area," Arizona real estate agent Lisa Bayless said.

According to a Zillow analysis of active listings across 606 ZIP codes with a Costco warehouse, roughly 3% explicitly highlight the store in their descriptions.

"Sellers are actively marketing proximity to the warehouse club as a selling point, treating it more like a lifestyle amenity," Zillow home trends expert Amanda Pendleton told USA TODAY.

In Pensacola, Florida, a recent listing for a three-bedroom cul-de-sac home touted its 20-minute drive to downtown and 30-minute commute to beaches right alongside the fact that Pensacola's first-ever Costco was opening just 2.6 miles away.

In Austin, Sean McCormack has built his 21-year membership into a core marketing strategy.

The broker-owner of Nice Move Realty offers customized searches on his website filtering homes by their radius to local Costcos and regional grocery giant H-E-B.

For McCormack, it's not just a sales gimmick. A Costco less than 10 minutes from his family home is a necessity with three boys aged 9 to 17.

"I thought it would be a cute idea to differentiate myself," he said. "It's for people who care about saving time and saving money."

That balance is why losing his local warehouse hit Staley so hard.

His Kansas City Costco recently closed to transition into a Costco business center that caters to commercial buyers rather than household shoppers so no more food court or free samples , he says. The next closest traditional warehouse is a 25-minute drive across the busy metro area so, at least for now, Staley will have to trade his near-daily Costco habit for longer-range planning as moving again isn't on the table.

"If it was just us and we didn't have kids to think about, it might be a different consideration," he said, citing local schools for keeping his family in place. "I'm going to have to go through some withdrawal there and get better at making sure I get everything on that one trip."

articles.title: Celtic fan banned for two years over Shankland gesture
articles.summary: Liam Connolly, 37, entered the Celtic Park pitch after his side were victorious against the Edinburgh club on 16 May.
articles.body:
A Celtic fan who made an offensive gesture to ex-Hearts player Lawrence Shankland during a pitch invasion has been banned from football matches for two years and ordered to do unpaid work.

Liam Connolly, 37, entered the Celtic Park pitch after his side were victorious against the Edinburgh club on 16 May, a result that clinched the league title for the Hoops.

He went on to approach then Hearts striker Shankland, 31, and made an "offensive gesture" towards him.

Connolly pleaded guilty at Glasgow Sheriff Court to committing breach of the peace.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

Celtic defeated Hearts 3-1 in a final day top of the table clash which meant the home side went on to win their 56th league title.

After the game, there was a mass pitch invasion from home fans.

Court papers said Connolly, of Kirkcaldy, Fife, conducted himself in a disorderly manner.

The charge said he formed part of a disorderly crowd and entered the field of play, before making the gesture to Shankland.

The supporter was carrying a child unknown to the Crown during the incident.

He was ordered to do 150 hours of unpaid work and banned from football matches for two years.

articles.title: Scientists discover ‘hidden materials’ that may lead to better batteries and solar fuels
articles.summary: An international research team has uncovered a class of previously unknown “hidden materials” by tracking the elusive, split-second changes that occur as
articles.body: An international research team has uncovered a class of previously unknown “hidden materials” by tracking the elusive, split-second changes that occur as molecules decompose under heat. The findings, published in Nature Communications, may unlock new pathways to develop more efficient solar fuel systems and higher-capacity batteries.Why this discovery is importantTypically, when materials scientists create solid compounds through thermal processing, attention is paid almost entirely to the final outcome – which is essentially moving straight from starting material “A” to end product “B.” However, by freezing and analysing the fleeting intermediate phases that arise during the heating cycle, researchers discovered entirely new structures that are difficult or impossible to manufacture using standard synthesis methods.“When materials are made by heating, scientists usually focus on the final product, the 'B' that results from 'A.' But this study shows that there are many fascinating stages in between 'A' and 'B,' and these hidden steps could be just as important,” said Dr. Sebastian Pike from the Department of Chemistry at the University of Warwick.“We didn't know exactly what we would find going in, but we were confident there would be something interesting and unknown in the intermediate phases. We were thrilled to discover that some of these could have practical uses, even from the very first experiments,” Pike added.Uncovering 'new form' of Bismuth VanadateThe team began their experiments using customised “single-source precursors” – single molecules engineered to contain every fundamental element required to yield a targeted solid material. As temperatures steadily rose, the scientists monitored how the molecular bonds broke apart and reassembled. This tracking exposed several uncharted material phases, most notably a newly discovered, kinetically stabilized form of bismuth vanadate.Standard bismuth vanadate has been prized in renewable energy engineering due to its optimal “band gap” – the exact energy threshold needed to absorb sunlight and catalyze chemical reactions. This characteristic allows it to harvest solar energy efficiently while providing the required chemical punch to split water molecules into clean hydrogen fuel.The newly identified ‘form’ features a distinct atomic architecture that sets it apart from all previously cataloged variations of the compound. Crucially, it possesses a significantly wider band gap, fundamentally changing how the material absorbs and reacts to light. Researchers note that this shift introduces fresh avenues to fine-tune materials across catalysis, advanced electronics, and solar fuel generation.Promising breakthrough for next-generation batteriesThe utility of these intermediate materials extends beyond solar energy. During the testing process, the scientists isolated another transient phase exhibiting high-capacity lithium storage, suggesting immediate promise for next-generation battery architectures.“What's exciting is that these 'in-between' materials aren't just stepping stones — they can have useful properties in their own right,” explained Dr. Dominik Kubicki from the School of Chemistry at the University of Birmingham. “By understanding and controlling how they form, we can start to design better materials for batteries, catalysis, and solar energy.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
articles.summary: William Chapman was attacked by the tiger after he entered its pen at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.
articles.body:
The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".

William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".

It said it was for the coroner to decide whether his mental illness played a part in his death, asking that the public respect that process.

City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death and the park remains closed.

"William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.

The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time".

"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued.

"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."

A spokesperson for the South Yorkshire Police said Chapman's family are being supported by specialist officers.

The incident, which took place shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday, led to the evacuation and ongoing closure of the park.

An eyewitness described seeing Chapman wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in.

Mobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass.

Chapman was a former pupil of the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe.

"We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us," the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe said in a tribute on Tuesday.

"It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him."

"Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with William's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time," the statement continued.

As a child, Chapman appeared in the ITV production May Contain Nuts alongside Shirley Henderson - who is best known for playing Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter films - and Darren Boyd.

He also portrayed Edward Jenner in the BBC series True Stories.

Staff at Yorkshire Wildlife Park have separately said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" are with Chapman's family and confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.

Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to Chapman's family and those who were at the scene.

articles.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer after surgery to remove part of lung
articles.summary: The 71-year-old is recovering in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after surgery to remove a cancerous growth on his lung.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican.

Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican added, noting the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests. It did not provide details on the recovery outlook or course of treatment.

In a statement released Tuesday, the Vatican said the procedure lasted 90 minutes and that the surgery “was successful, and there were no complications”.

The 71-year-old has returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he is expected to recover for a week, with all his audiences through October 20 cancelled.

The Vatican said doctors are not currently discussing chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests.

The Holy See’s press office noted the medical statement spoke of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in the hope of eliminating any lingering traces of the cancer.

Before the procedure, Leo waved to dozens of well-wishers gathered at the hospital’s main entrance.

In an unusually transparent update on papal health, Leo first revealed that doctors found a small nodule during his Sunday noon prayer in St Peter’s Square.

“The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I’ve decided to have surgery to remove it,” he said during remarks delivered in Italian.

The pope has no reported history of serious illness and is considered physically active, routinely swimming and playing tennis.

The surgery comes ahead of an official Latin America tour scheduled for November 6-17, with stops planned across Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

It is unclear whether his recovery will affect the ambitious itinerary, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and significant altitude changes in Peru.

The pope told reporters on Sunday that he intends to make the journey.

articles.title: George Washington spent much of his childhood at Ferry Farm; after Walmart bought the Virginia property in 1996, locals raised $2.2 million to save it and donated it to a nonprofit foundation
articles.summary: Thirty years ago, the historic site of George Washington’s childhood home in Virginia came close to being transformed into a Walmart Supercenter, until
articles.body: Thirty years ago, the historic site of George Washington’s childhood home in Virginia came close to being transformed into a Walmart Supercenter, until local residents rallied to save the property. Known as Ferry Farm, the site was purchased by the retail giant in 1996 for a proposed development, prompting concerns among community members about the loss of an important piece of American history. Residents organised campaigns, raised awareness and eventually collected $2.2 million to buy back the land. The property was subsequently donated to the George Washington Foundation, preserving the site where the first US president spent much of his childhood.How George Washington’s childhood home was savedWashington moved to Ferry Farm with his family when he was six years old. After his father died when he was 11, the young Washington inherited the farm and took on greater responsibilities within his family.The property played an important role in his formative years, introducing him to agriculture and land surveying. These skills later helped him establish a career as a surveyor in Culpeper County, Virginia, before he joined the militia and eventually became the first president of the United States.Despite its historical significance, Ferry Farm remained unprotected for years. In 1996, Walmart purchased the property with plans to build a Supercenter, according to WJLA. The development was initially welcomed by county officials, who were looking for ways to increase tax revenue.However, the proposal prompted a backlash among residents who believed that the historic land deserved protection.“And locals said, ‘Wait a minute, this isn't right,’” Heidi Bass, a Fredericksburg, Virginia, business owner, told WJLA.Residents launch a grassroots campaignAmong those who opposed the proposed development was Cessie Howell, who recalled refusing to accept that the historic site would be lost to commercial construction.“So many people would say, ‘It's a done deal.’ It's been signed, it's a done deal.’ And I just kept thinking, it just can't be a done deal. It can't be. George Washington, our hero, to have a Walmart next door,” Howell said.She and other advocates began organising a grassroots campaign to save the property. They advertised in newspapers, held community meetings and worked to draw attention to the site's historical importance.“We just started advertising in the paper and we had meetings here. It was right around George Washington's birthday, and people like you came and made it an important issue,” Howell told WJLA.She also credited television coverage with helping spread awareness of the campaign beyond the local community.“Had we not had stations like your station, we would not be where we are today because it spread across the United States,” she said.How the community raised $2.2 millionAs opposition to the Walmart development gained momentum, residents and supporters raised $2.2 million to buy back the property. Walmart ultimately accepted the offer, allowing the land to be transferred to the Kenmore Foundation, now known as the George Washington Foundation.The successful campaign became an example of how community action and public awareness can help preserve historically significant places threatened by commercial development.Reflecting on the outcome, Howell expressed gratitude to the people who contributed to the effort.“I'm just thankful that all these people came together and saved it,” she said.Ferry Farm’s historical significanceFerry Farm was designated a National Historic Landmark in 2000, four years after the campaign to save it began. The designation recognises the site's historical importance and raises its profile, although it does not automatically prevent commercial development.For historians and archaeologists, the property offers an opportunity to understand Washington's early life beyond the familiar story of his military and political achievements.The oldest remaining building on the property is a small shed dating to the 1870s. In 2008, archaeologists discovered the structural foundation of the house where Washington spent his childhood. A replica of the home was completed a decade later and opened to the public in 2018.The reconstructed house allows visitors to explore the domestic environment in which Washington grew up and learn about the everyday experiences that shaped his early years.Visitors can experience Washington’s childhood homeToday, Ferry Farm operates as a historic attraction where visitors can explore the reconstructed house and learn about life during Washington's childhood.Allison Burgess, director of education at the George Washington Foundation, said the site offers an interactive experience designed to help visitors connect with history.“Ferry Farm is one of the most family friendly museums you're going to find in the area. When you go in the Washington house, you don't have to worry about saying, ‘please don't touch that.’ You're allowed to touch anything because we want you to interact with the entire experience in the house,” Burgess said.She explained that visitors are encouraged to sit on the beds and chairs, examine the table settings and engage with the furnishings rather than simply observing them from a distance.“We want you to sit on the bed and test out the rope beds. We want you to sit in the chairs, pull up a chair to the dining room table. Look at the silverware on the tables. It's a very interactive experience,” she added.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Tuesday said that if China wants a normal relationship with New Delhi, the border between the two
articles.body: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Tuesday said that if China wants a normal relationship with New Delhi, the border between the two countries has to be stable.During a conversation at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, Jaishankar said that India and China do not have an agreed border and that the issue has persisted for decades."We don't have an agreed border between India and China. This is not a new issue; it's been going on for multiple decades... From 1975 till 2020, a good 45 years, no blood was shed on that border. The last time there were fatalities was in 1975. In this period, India-China relations did grow," he said."Then in 2020, when we were in the midst of the Covid lockdown, we had a series of border issues, and it culminated in a clash in which a number of soldiers were killed on either side," Jaishankar added.Jaishankar said that if peace and tranquillity in the border areas are disturbed, then the relationship will have consequences."For us, what it represented was a very profound departure from the situation that was prevailing since 1975. If the peace and tranquillity in the border areas are disturbed, then the relationship will have consequences. Those consequences were very visible for the next five years until we were able to restore the peace and tranquillity. It took four years of negotiations," he added."The point we make to the Chinese is: 'If you want a normal relationship, if the rest of the relationship is to move, it's common sense. It's a no-brainer that the boundary has to be stable, that we need peace and tranquillity in the border areas.' As the border areas are settling down, they have settled down to a great extent since 2024; the relationship is commensurately moving towards normalcy," he further said.This comes after the ministry of external affairs reiterated that the Union territory of Ladakh is an integral and inalienable part of India after the Chinese foreign ministry opposed the naming of certain strategic locations in Ladakh."The announcement mentions that the twenty-eight (28) places/features located in the UT of Ladakh have been identified with standard place and feature names on the official map of Survey of India, and it has been done in consultation with the Union Territory of Ladakh and local stakeholders," MEA said."Identifying these places formally on the Survey of India map of UT of Ladakh is aimed at facilitating their accurate recognition and better awareness among the public at large," the ministry said.On October 2, India formally identified 28 strategic locations and geographical features in Ladakh on its official map, including key border friction points along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), such as Gogra and Hot Spring.The move, undertaken in consultation with the Ladakh administration, aimed to improve official mapping, ensure precise identification and raise public awareness of the sensitive border region.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Tim Walz warns Democrats will face reckoning if they win power and fail to deliver change
articles.summary: Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz warns Democrats will face serious backlash if they win back power but fail to deliver on housing and college education.
articles.body: Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz issued a warning to his party in an interview Thursday, arguing there would be backlash if Democrats win elections in November and beyond but fail to make significant structural changes. During an interview with "The Lever" founder David Sirota, Walz was asked if the Democratic Party had an issue offering up big promises but ultimately failing to deliver. "Yes, a hundred percent. It’s a hundred percent," Walz said. "I always use the line, as I said, we win these elections not to bank the political capital to win the next one but to improve lives. We’re too slow about it. And some of that is structural," WATCH: DEMOCRATS ADMIT WHEN THEY'D ELIMINATE THE FILIBUSTER AS SAVE ACT FIGHT HEATS UP He pointed to former Sen. Joe Manchin's position that the filibuster must remain in place in the Senate. "Look, I’m friends with Joe Manchin, but the desire to hold onto the filibuster at all costs as an institution when it had real impacts on people’s lives of real important things, and by not doing that, it played right into the hands of the Republicans. I think we’re not responsive, and then we fall into that 'But we voted for you, and you didn’t get anything done,'" Walz said. Manchin has been consistent in his support for the filibuster. In 2022, he and then-Sen. Kyrsten Sinema voted against changing the Senate's 60-vote threshold for advancing most legislation, opposing other Democrats who sought to change the rules to pass voting legislation. WALZ APPROVAL RATING CRATERS TO LOWEST LEVEL EVER AND TRAILS TRUMP AMID MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL: 'TIRED OF IT' Walz, the 2024 Democratic vice presidential nominee, warned of a "real danger." "Here’s where I think the real danger is. If there is not significant structural change — whether it’s inequities, you know, income inequities or opportunities — the backlash, because, I said this: I got into politics because I said we’ll never find a worse president than George Bush. And I think now, if you think that this is the pinnacle of how bad things can get, I would caution you to rethink that. "And especially if Democrats do all of this, the public turns out, they vote for us and kids still can’t afford a college education, can’t afford housing. That’s going to be a problem." He then predicted that Democrats would regain control of the House, Senate and eventually the presidency in 2028. MN LAWMAKERS UNLOAD ON WALZ'S 'LEGACY' AFTER HE TOUTS FRAUD RECORD IN FINAL ANNUAL ADDRESS: 'RIDICULOUS' Lindsey Drath, CEO of the Forward Party, told Fox News Digital, "We shouldn't advocate for abolishing the filibuster to drive home party-line votes with no effort to advance cross-partisan consensus law making. What hampers Congress' ability to deliver material solutions to the American people is a two-party system that penalizes working across the aisle. "This circular dynamic, whereby Democrats or Republicans enter into a narrow majority, only to focus on maintaining power, accumulates a kind of figurative debt against the challenges facing the American people," she said. "This dynamic pushes our elected officials away from working on real solutions for actual problems and toward whatever hyper polarized means by which they can to hold on to power. "This is why a fulcrum strategy is key," Drath continued. "The Senate today passes almost nothing on a bipartisan basis, not because the problems aren't solvable, but because neither party has any incentive to negotiate. Every compromise is a political cost. If someone crosses the aisle, they are attacked by their party. It is framed as every deal made is a loss to play at home. The incentive is to obstruct, posture and wait for the next election. "The fulcrum strategy is that you don't need a majority to change the Senate," she added. "You need only a handful. It uses a small bloc of independents to balance power in Congress and take away full majority from either side. With an expected closely divided Congress this cycle, this is very relevant and real. It would mean both parties would have to negotiate with those few in the middle before anything passes. The party that wants their vote has to offer something real, something that actually serves the people." He reflected on his tenure as governor in a September interview, including his handling of widespread fraud involving Minnesota social services programs. "Fraud — should have stopped it sooner," Walz told The Minnesota Star Tribune. "We didn’t stop them. I accept that. I think there does need to be accountability with that. And part of it is that, yep, that’s with me, I’ll step aside." The governor said the state "immediately" took action to address the fraud and then suggested that the true cost of the fraud, estimated at $9 billion by federal prosecutors, has been overstated. Walz also compared the fraud losses to the cost of President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom, which he suggested was more expensive. "I should have been down on those agencies a little more, but I will tell you this, in the scheme of things, all the fraud that's been prosecuted, by the way, and all the fraud that's probably out there is less than the ballroom at the White House," Walz said. "So, it puts it into perspective. It doesn't make it right. Doesn't make it right." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Andrew Mark Miller contributed to this report.

articles.title: Embattled Soros-backed DA blames ‘criminal’ police misconduct in accused Philly cop killer’s prior murder case
articles.summary: Eric Lewis was acquitted of murder in 2019 after what DA Larry Krasner says was police misconduct that deeply undermined the earlier homicide case.
articles.body: Eric Lewis, the man accused of killing a Philadelphia police officer in an ambush, was acquitted of murder in 2019 in a case the district attorney says was undermined by police misconduct. Lewis, 35, is accused of fatally shooting Philadelphia Police Officer Shane Seiber and wounding his partner. He now faces a range of charges, among them murder, homicide of a law enforcement officer, attempted murder, 10 counts of attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer, aggravated assault, terroristic threats and other related offenses. He In a video statement Tuesday, Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner said Lewis was acquitted in an earlier murder case and blamed police misconduct for the outcome. "Why this man was out of custody? The answer is this, this man is out of custody because a balanced, good and fair judge did what he had to do because two absolutely excellent prosecutors did everything humanly possible with a case and an investigation that was so deeply flawed. It was not just full of errors and mistakes, very serious ones, But some of the conduct involving one police officer... And one detective is arguably criminal. Yes, I said criminal," Krasner said. articles.title: DGCA bans a particular powerbank on all flights
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has barred a particular powerbank from being carried on aircraft in either passenger or cargo
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has barred a particular powerbank from being carried on aircraft in either passenger or cargo flights to, from and within India.The decision came in view of the "recent fire incident involving the MOBIKINS MK-PB-04 powerbank, and considering the potential safety risks associated with it", the regulatory body said.An IndiGo flight from Delhi to Chennai was diverted to Hyderabad Sunday after a passenger's personal electronic device caught fire.An order issued by DGCA chief Vir Vikram Yadav said the "travelling public and airlines" were advised to ensure that the MOBIKINS MK-PB-04 powerbank was not carried or transported on board the aircraft."Airlines are further advised to take appropriate measures to identify and prevent the carriage of the aforesaid powerbank and to disseminate this safety advisory to the passengers through suitable communication channels," the order said.Over the past year, several countries, including India, have started restricting powerbank usage on aircraft due to the possibility of them catching fire. Apart from limiting the number of powerbanks and their battery capacity, they can neither be used to charge personal electronic devices nor be charged via the in-seat power source on aircraft.Instances of PED and powerbank fires have been on the rise globally. The biggest scare here remains airlines taking cabin bags from passengers at the boarding gate to be kept in the baggage hold. If a fire breaks out in the belly baggage hold, it may be a while before it is detected.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Missing head of Khajuraho idol will be restored soon: ASI chief
articles.summary: The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) has found the missing head of an 11th-century Vishnu idol at Khajuraho, whose restoration became the subject of a
articles.body: The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) has found the missing head of an 11th-century Vishnu idol at Khajuraho, whose restoration became the subject of a recent controversy involving the Supreme Court, and plans to reattach it after expert examination. ASI has also introduced a three-year deadline for archaeological excavations to curb delays in research and cut approval times for most conservation projects to 15-20 days, director general Yadubir Singh Rawat told TOI in an exclusive interview. He also revealed plans for a preliminary excavation at Ujjain's Vaishya Tekri, where a Buddhist stupa could be larger than Sanchi's, although its actual scale and significance remain to be established.Controversy over the beheaded Vishnu idol at Khajuraho's Javari temple reached the Supreme Court last year when advocate Rakesh Dalal sought restoration, replacement or reconstruction of the seven-foot statue. While dismissing the petition, then CJI BR Gavai had said, "Go and ask the deity itself to do something now." Though Gavai later said he respects all religions and that his statement was taken out of context, a lawyer had tried to throw a shoe at him inside the courtroom.Rawat said the missing head had been found in an ASI store. "During a visit to Bhopal for the Brics summit, I learnt that the statue's head - which had been kept in our store - had been found. The person in charge informed me that someone likely tried to break off the head to steal it but failed to do so. We are having experts examine it and will soon reattach it to the statue."On encroachments at protected monuments, Rawat said "The root of this problem lies in the list prepared by British rulers in 1904 under the 'Ancient Monuments Preservation Act' - a list that the then govt adopted post-Independence without any review. The British had included cemeteries and graves of their obscure soldiers, horses and pets - which they deemed highly significant - among protected monuments." Rawat said a review in 1953 incorporated state monuments into a definitive list, but the central list remained unchanged. The resulting difficulties led to 17 monuments being removed from it.Regarding funding disparities, he said allocations depended on visitor numbers, maintenance requirements, security expenses and public facilities. Taj Mahal and Red Fort, he said, served as showcases for ASI, while Taj Mahal's maintenance required substantial expenditure because of its delicate structure and heavy tourist footfall. ASI paid around Rs 3 crore monthly for more than 200 CISF personnel deployed there.He said ASI circles had been instructed to prepare conservation and tourism development proposals for lesser-known sites like Bareilly's pyramid-like Bhim ki Gada structure.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Woman accused of deadly revenge crash faces jury as boyfriend’s hospital account stays out of trial
articles.summary: Leigha Mumby's trial opened with prosecutors alleging she turned sharply into woods at nearly 100 mph after a fight over another girl's texts.
articles.body: A Florida woman accused of deliberately crashing an SUV with her boyfriend inside was furious over another girl’s text messages before making a sharp turn into the woods at nearly 100 mph, prosecutors told jurors Tuesday. But Leigha Mumby’s defense attorney offered a different explanation as her trial opened, suggesting something happened inside the vehicle that she neither anticipated nor controlled. Mumby, 25, has pleaded not guilty to vehicular homicide and reckless driving causing serious bodily injury in the death of Daniel Waterman, 22, who survived the crash, but died eight months later. Assistant State Attorney Melissa Clark told jurors the couple had left a Super Bowl party before the Feb. 9, 2025, wreck on Interstate 95 in Flagler County, according to proceedings livestreamed by Court TV. OHIO SUPREME COURT DENIES MACKENZIE SHIRILLA'S LATEST APPEAL BID IN DOUBLE MURDER CASE Clark said the SUV traveled at speeds exceeding 100 mph before the crash. Vehicle data showed it was moving at 94 mph in the final seconds before an "abrupt, left-hand turn at 45 degrees" sent it off the highway and into the woods. The prosecutor described the turn as "a dangerous and reckless maneuver." Waterman suffered a broken neck that left him paralyzed from the neck down, Clark said. He fell into a coma and, after awakening, could not breathe on his own. His death on Oct. 8, 2025, was "directly related and caused by this crash," Clark told the jury, who will not hear Waterman's own account of the crash that he told detectives before he died. He told investigators from his hospital bed that Mumby deliberately swerved off the road following an argument over another woman's text message. A judge ruled those statements inadmissible, leaving prosecutors unable to present his version of events at trial. Defense attorney Reid Hart called the case a "pure and utter tragedy" and urged jurors to consider whether the SUV’s sudden change in direction resulted from something outside Mumby’s control. "The crux of this trial effectively comes down to one steering wheel input, and ultimately one question," Hart said, according to Court TV’s livestream. Hart questioned whether Mumby chose to drive off the road or whether something happened inside the vehicle that "she did not expect, she did not anticipate, and she did not control." He argued that once the vehicle began careening toward the woods, she could not stop it despite trying to avoid the crash. MACKENZIE SHIRILLA'S TEXTS SURFACE AS 'HELL ON WHEELS' DRIVER'S APPEAL COLLIDES WITH NETFLIX'S 'THE CRASH' Jurors also heard Tuesday from Sarah Stappenbeck, Waterman’s cousin and Mumby’s best friend, who hosted the Super Bowl gathering. Stappenbeck testified that Mumby announced earlier that day that she had learned she was pregnant. But the news came alongside concerns about Waterman’s contact with other women. Mumby "expressed concerns of Daniel talking to other girls and said that she wasn’t going to let Daniel cheat on her," Stappenbeck testified. The couple left before the game ended. Within about 20 minutes, Stappenbeck said, Mumby called her, yelling that Waterman was texting another girl and that she planned to bring him back to the house. "She’s yelling at me," Stappenbeck recalled. WATCH: MACKENZIE SHIRILLA’S FATHER CALLS HER ‘A DUMB 18-YEAR-OLD’ WHILE BERATING POLICE IN BODYCAM VIDEO Stappenbeck said she did not hear Waterman speaking in the background. She tried to calm Mumby and urged the couple to get home safely and address their disagreement the following day. "She just said that ‘You’re taking his side,’ and hung up with me," Stappenbeck testified. About 20 minutes later, Mumby called again, still angry, and repeated that she was bringing Waterman back, Stappenbeck said. They never arrived. Instead, Stappenbeck testified, Mumby’s roommate called and told her to go to the hospital because there had been a crash. The trial is unfolding without Waterman’s account to investigators of what happened inside the SUV. Before his death, Waterman told detectives Mumby deliberately caused the wreck after an argument over a text from another woman, according to charging documents previously reported by Court TV. He said the last thing he remembered was Mumby telling him, "I don’t care what happens, you’ll get what you deserve," before swerving off the road. Judge Dawn Nichols ruled those statements could not be introduced at trial. Prosecutors said they wanted jurors to hear Waterman’s account, but acknowledged the rules of evidence prevented them from using it at trial, Court TV previously reported. "The court is bound by the law and the court is bound by the rules of evidence," Nichols said when explaining the ruling. The first day of Mumby’s trial also brought an emotional moment for Waterman’s family. His mother, Heather Waterman, was seen wiping away tears as a photo of her son was shown in court. Court adjourned for the day following Tuesday’s proceedings. Mumby was initially arrested in July 2025 on charges of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon. FAMILY OF FATHER-TO-BE WHOSE GIRLFRIEND ALLEGEDLY CRASHED CAR ON PURPOSE SPEAKS OUT THROUGH LAWYER After Waterman died, prosecutors upgraded her charges to include vehicular homicide. She was booked into the Flagler County Jail and released after posting a $150,000 bond. Waterman’s mother previously told Syracuse.com that he spent time in a coma before recovering enough to tell investigators what happened. Waterman’s aunt, Tiffany Waterman, expressed anguish over the exclusion of her nephew’s statements in a Facebook post Monday as jury selection began. She remembered his efforts to comfort a loved one watching a movie beside him in his hospital bed, smiling at her while trying to conceal his pain. "That’s who Daniel was. Protective, loving, and sweet," she wrote. "He had the biggest heart, even in those last moments of life." The family previously told Fox News Digital through attorney John Hager that they supported the charges filed following Waterman’s death. "There are no real winners in this situation. It’s a terrible, horrible situation," Hager said in November 2025, adding that the family believed the charges were "right and just." Mumby gave birth to a baby girl three days after Waterman died, according to WSYR. "Daniel was an excited, soon-to-be father of a baby girl," his obituary said. "He wanted nothing more than to come home to her and to the family who loved him so dearly." Similar case The trial comes amid renewed attention to another deadly crash involving a young woman convicted of intentionally driving into a building with her boyfriend inside. Mackenzie Shirilla is serving two concurrent sentences of 15 years to life for killing her boyfriend, Dominic Russo, 20, and their friend, Davion Flanagan, 19, in a 2022 crash in Strongsville, Ohio, Fox News Digital previously reported. Shirilla’s case became the subject of Netflix’s "The Crash." She was convicted in 2023 after prosecutors argued she deliberately drove into a brick building at nearly 100 mph to end her relationship with Russo. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Ohio Supreme Court recently rejected her request to reconsider its decision, declining to hear her latest appeal. Shirilla has maintained the crash was not intentional. Fox News Digital's Michael Sinkewicz, Greg Norman, and Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

articles.title: More tea? How Scotland's crops of the future could be set to change
articles.summary: Experts are examining the ways Scotland's farmers might diversify and adapt to a changing climate.
articles.body:
Susie Walker-Munro is one of a handful of tea growers in Scotland.

She says the acidic soil creates ideal conditions for the perfect artisan brew.

Costing about £40 per packet for her most expensive product, it's not going to replace the supermarket brands any time soon.

Droughts, intensive downpours and diseases have created challenges for tea growers across the world as they deal with the impact of a warming planet.

But some experts believe Scotland's relatively settled climate could give the tea industry here a helping hand.

As the picking season draws to a close, Susie plucks the last few leaves before proudly pouring me a small glass of her Kinnettles Gold, which is grown in a walled garden on the family farm near Forfar.

She believes Scotland's latitude – sitting 57 degrees north - will always be a bar to having a year-round crop like those countries close to the equator.

But she says wetter weather could help boost production.

"Our yields are never, never going to be high," she says.

"Maybe with climate change they might come up a bit, it depends if we get enough rain. Scotland could be absolutely ideal."

Susie isn't convinced tea will ever be a major crop for Scotland.

But others say it could be one of a numbers of options in the future, as farmers are forced to diversify and adapt to a changing climate.

Rethinking the way we farm the land might be one way to extend the range of crops produced.

Countries like the Netherlands are already embracing glass houses, which could become more commonplace in Scotland. Susie says they would be a good way of growing more tea.

They would also allow Scotland to produce more Mediterranean vegetables like tomatoes, cucumbers, aubergines, and even melons, according to Pete Ritchie from campaign organisation Nourish Scotland.

He says an abundance of renewable energy from wind farms later in the century will make heating them relatively cheap and will cut down on air miles.

"We're going to be able to produce those plants with a lower carbon footprint and provide secure all-round jobs for people on brownfield sites in the cities and also on the islands and remote parts of Scotland," he says.

The James Hutton Institute already has a large number of glass houses – but it is going even further by artificially creating the sort of conditions that may exist in 75 years.

Climate modelling shows that Scotland can expect hotter, dryer summers and milder, wetter winters by the end of this century.

The institute's new advanced plant growth centre is effectively a climate simulator.

It's able to control plants' light, water and nutrient intake to test how they cope with stresses - and then select species which are likely to fare best against all that climate change can throw at them.

For the past three months they have been experimenting with fava beans, which are photographed daily so scientists can monitor their progress.

Dr Robert Hancock says they need to switch from breeding crops for specific environments, such as hot or dry climates, towards ones which are more generally resilient.

"We need to start breeding those crops now and start understanding what Scottish farming's going to look like," he says.

"Farmers need time to plan, we need to get those crops out to the farmers and registered.

"Ultimately it's about what those guys do in the fields that matters, not what we do inside a climate simulator."

The farmers of the 22nd Century are probably only a generation away from those starting out in the industry today.

That means the current crop of young farmers will have to give the closest consideration to the businesses they hand on to their own children.

And that means more precision farming, more artificial intelligence, and automation.

Modern tractors and combine harvesters are so high in technology such as GPS steering that it's no longer such a leap to consider autonomous harvesting.

But the chair of the Scottish Association of Young Farmers, David Murdoch, believes traditional skills will always be important.

"There's no point in doing it if you don't know your cattle, but embracing the technology is what keeps us competitive.

"Working with larger herd numbers and larger machinery to keep us producing more with less people - that's the way the world's going," says David, who farms dairy with his father at Beith in North Ayrshire.

But it's not just food production that will drive future changes in farming.

Protecting and enhancing nature, offsetting carbon emissions, and renewable energy production are already shaping the farms of tomorrow.

Health innovations may also play a growing role, with obesity drugs already showing a demand for proteins and nutrient-dense foods.

Soya, flax and legumes could become a more common sight as conditions for growing them become more favourable and that desire to grow them locally continues.

Prof Wayne Powell - the principal of Scotland's rural college, the SRUC - predicts that Scotland will become "the bread basket of Europe".

That title is currently used to describe Ukraine, because of its abundance of fertile agricultural land and exports of crops including wheat, maize and barley.

"Climate change is redrawing the farming map of Europe and Scotland could become one of Europe's most important climate resilient food regions," he says.

"The possibility of access to cheap renewable energy could also transform the economics of Scottish farming from irrigation, refrigeration, food processing, so that we can capture more value from our land and food."

Scotland's rural communities have seen major changes over the past 75 years which have resulted in far fewer people working the land.

Pressure to keep food affordable for consumers while farms remain profitable will be a key driver of innovation.

The changing climate and the continued destruction of our nature prevent that being a simple equation to calculate.

But farmers are used to change – in the short, medium and long-term - and by the end of the century our fields will probably be as unrecognisable to today's farmers as all those who have gone before them.

articles.title: Haze: Who's to blame for the toxic smog choking South East Asia?
articles.summary: Anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning land in Indonesia and the authorities who have failed to stop them.
articles.body:
As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region.

The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra have turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels.

The smog - also known as the haze - has also drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia.

Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland - as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them.

The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El Niño - a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world.

According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land.

Many of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn".

This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops.

But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.

While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky.

But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders.

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism".

Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed.

But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy amid the haze problem.

A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning.

This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace.

First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implement robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations".

Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded.

Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished.

"We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said.

'When there is no smoke, we send oxygen'

It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies.

In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze.

The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law.

But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies.

Also in 2015, Indonesia's then-Vice-President Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset".

Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads Indonesia's government communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".

"When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans.

But Indonesia has in the past also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze.

This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires - though it has not officially requested international support.

In Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society to force the government to take action.

In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze.

They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the coverage of healthcare costs.

A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra, but it was dismissed.

Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have remained at dangerous levels for weeks.

There are many who have no choice but to brave the toxic smog every day.

"I'm short of breath and have a headache breathing air now. But I still have to work," Imrayedi, a 63-year-old motorcycle taxi driver in Pekanbaru city, on Sumatra island, told BBC Indonesian last week.

"The government must also think about the common people like us. Please take action to find a solution so that this haze problem can be resolved immediately."
