articles.title: Paid companionship grows as loneliness rises in China
articles.summary: As loneliness grows in China, a new industry is emerging to provide companionship and support.
articles.body:
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."

Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia.

"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."

Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.

Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".

There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.

But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.

Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that.

"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs.

"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine."

"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.

Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.

The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.

His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.

There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.

Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile.

"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.

She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.

But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood.

"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.

Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.

Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic.

"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."

She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves.

"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."

At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.

Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee.

"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."

Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province.

"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.

The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.

He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said.

"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."

After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude.

"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback."

Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity.

Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly.

"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said.

"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy.

"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

articles.title: Pakistan has locked down Imran Khan's stronghold - but it could backfire
articles.summary: Some fear the government's standoff with the former PM's supporters could bring more instability, not less.
articles.body:
Schools closed. The internet partially shut. Roads blocked by shipping containers. And the army arriving in town.

Imran Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is under a state of emergency, his party's provincial government suspended. It's another dramatic escalation in the standoff between the former prime minister's supporters and Pakistan's state - and one that some fear could lead to more instability, not less.

According to the federal government this step, allowed by the constitution, was needed to provide protection for the province's population from the threat of terror.

"The PTI KPK government was hand in glove with the terrorists," Attah Tarrar, federal information minister, told journalists on Sunday. He did not elaborate or provide evidence, but promised to do so soon.

Two days later there had still been no update from him - but schools had reopened in Peshawar and most parts of the province, and internet services had been restored.

While police would not confirm any detentions, there is clearly a crackdown under way to prevent protests. Most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding.

On Tuesday dozens of PTI supporters took to the streets in Bara, Khyber district, hometown of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. There were reports of tear gas shelling in the area.

To many observers, the timing of Sunday's announcement of emergency rule is not coincidental.

For the last week, thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have marched through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa , where the PTI have been in power for 13 years, demanding Khan's release.

"The charitable response would be to say that it sounded disingenuous," says Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House.

"I do not see the link with terrorism," says Arifa Noor, journalist and commentator. "I'm not even sure if it was the long march itself [that led to this]. Perhaps it was the last straw or perhaps it's just a case of saying, we don't want to deal with the government being in the hands of an opposition party."

The protests were led by Chief Minister Afridi, whose whereabouts are still a mystery. His party says he has been arrested; the government says that he is in protective custody.

Before the march had begun, there had been a crackdown. Three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September , accused among other things of mobilising supporters, and have been detained ever since.

Khan has barely been seen by his family or lawyers in the last year; two of his sisters saw him in August, one in prison, another as he was checked over at a hospital visit after concerns were raised by the Supreme Court about his health, before he was returned behind bars again where he has been held for more than three years.

The PTI leader, who is widely believed to have lost power because of a rift with Pakistan's powerful military, has been imprisoned since August 2023. He is convicted in several corruption cases which he says are politically motivated.

With the party already weakened, why this reaction from the authorities?

"The PTI rank and file has been becoming increasingly restless in recent months amid growing concerns about Imran Khan's health," says Michael Kugelman, senior South Asia fellow at the Atlantic Council.

"There is a sense that perhaps now is the time to send a very strong message to the party and make it more difficult for them to be able to put pressure on the government."

The government has previously argued that Khan was going against jail rules by using his meetings to discuss politics.

Tarar has said of the state of emergency: "There was no political agenda. They could have gone on with their march," and pointed to the talks the two sides had in the run-up to the decision as an indicator that they did try discussion.

But others see this as just another attempt to restrict Khan and his party.

"The government has less and less space for disagreements or dissent and they do not want to negotiate their way out of any kind of conflict," Noor says.

Zahid Hussain, Islamabad-based author and defence analyst, is clear about who is behind the decision.

"The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment," he says.

Sheikh thinks that Pakistan's military is feeling confident because it believes it has a good relationship with the White House, its international credentials burnished by their role in the US-Iran peace talks.

"The mode is very much, this is the moment, let's seize it," she says. "There is a sense that, we have all the cards in our hands. We can ride this out internationally."

Ex-cricket captains urge 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan

Imran Khan not the only one silenced as Pakistan military stifles dissent

The cricket star and former PM dividing Pakistan

But Pakistan has plenty to contend with. Militancy is rising. The country was ranked number one in the Global Terrorism Index 2026 as the country which had been affected most.

The country is at loggerheads with two neighbours; it has repeatedly hit Afghanistan with air strikes accusing the Afghan Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, a claim it denies. It would take little to reignite its long-running simmering conflict with India.

Meanwhile, it has promised to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks as the conflict against the Houthis has become increasingly dangerous.

Short of solving one problem, some have warned this state of emergency could lead to more challenges. It risks increasing political instability, with Islamabad taking responsibility for a province without a buffer - the provincial government - they can blame.

"I would argue that this could actually backfire," Kugelman says. "You're playing with fire because if this move ends up adding to the anger and the discontent among so many there, then you have a very big problem on your hands."

"It is reckless, given the challenges, multiple challenges the country is facing," Hussain says. He fears that more of these powers could be used across Pakistan.

Attempts to combat militancy with more active army operations could come with its own perils too, Sheikh argues.

"If they're going to launch these operations, they're going to have to be prepared to accept casualties of members of the armed forces," she says. If those are significant, it could lead to questions inside the military institution, she adds.

Pakistan, with its history of military coups, has examples in its past where removing elected governments, whether provincial or national, can turn sour.

"It's not that senior people in the PML-N [the party in federal government] don't realise that some of these things can come back and haunt them in the future," Noor says.

"Similarly I think to some extent the PTI realises that they will not be able to hold a protest and get Imran Khan out. I think that's the most unfortunate part of this mess that we're in, that we are going into it with our eyes wide open.

"Everybody realises that this is a train crash but somehow you can't stop it."

articles.title: A couple started a coffee cart using a $1,500 credit-card limit; their business now generates $4.5 million a year
articles.summary: Audrey Finocchiaro and Sam Lancaster started ‘The Nitro Bar’ in 2016 with a $1,500 credit card limit, scrap wood, and a plan to sell nitrogen-infused cold
articles.body: Audrey Finocchiaro and Sam Lancaster started ‘The Nitro Bar’ in 2016 with a $1,500 credit card limit, scrap wood, and a plan to sell nitrogen-infused cold brew coffee from a makeshift cart. The couple initially struggled to attract customers, earning just $20 to $60 during eight-hour days on the streets of Providence, Rhode Island.Their fortunes changed when they brought the cart to Brown University, where a queue of students helped transform the struggling venture into a promising business. Over time, the company expanded into wholesale, opened coffee shops, and gained traction on social media. According to an interview with Fortune, Finocchiaro revealed that the business generates $4.5 million in annual revenue.How a couple built a mobile coffee business with just $1,500In 2016, Finocchiaro and Lancaster used a $1,500 credit limit and scrap wood from her parents’ basement to build a basic coffee cart. The makeshift structure was little more than a box and had no electricity, with space only for the equipment needed to prepare their nitrogen-infused cold brew. The couple loaded it into Finocchiaro’s Subaru Outback and drove to Providence, Rhode Island, where they began selling coffee on city streets and at community events.They often set up stalls on their own initiative, hoping to attract customers, but initially earned just $20 to $60 over eight-hour days.Brown University students helped the coffee cart find customersThe turning point came when Lancaster realised they had not yet taken the cart to Brown University. When students returned to Brown University that autumn, the couple began attracting larger crowds, and their sales improved significantly. Finocchiaro recalled one day when a queue formed and they made about $600, a sum that felt life-changing at the time.The couple began visiting the university daily to serve undergraduates who gathered around the cart for cold brew. In spring 2017, two investors approached them at a Providence farmers’ market and asked how much funding they needed to expand. After working through financial projections together, they estimated they needed about $150,000.How did the couple use their $150,000 to expand their coffee business“The next day, we got that money, which was crazy,” said Finocchiaro. Until then, the couple had prepared their cold brew each night at her uncle’s diner. The funding allowed them to set up a production facility and expand into wholesale, which they hoped would help sustain the business during winter months.However, much of the money was quickly spent, including on kegerators for the 60 wholesale accounts they secured in their first year. Each unit cost $1,200 and allowed customers to dispense cold brew directly from a keg. The couple later found another opportunity when a local bike shop offered them 200 square feet of space for $400 a month. They used a Square loan with a 30% interest rate to open their first storefront.How Instagram and TikTok helped the couple grow their coffee business to $4.5 millionThe ‘Nitro Bar’ generates $4.5 million in annual revenue and employs 80 people across three coffee shops, a production facility, and a small coffee trailer. Its cold brew is also available on tap at more than 50 other locations in Rhode Island and Massachusetts. The company has built an audience of more than 500,000 followers on TikTok and 130,000 on Instagram.Finocchiaro said, “We just threw a ton of things at a wall and kept going until we found something that stuck”.“And for us, that took I think it was seven years until we really started to gain a significant following online.”“I think it’s an incredible time to start a business, because it can cost $0 to start”.“You can have no money and start a TikTok or start an Instagram account. That was monumental for us.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Albanian police fire tear gas at protesters as Education Ministry attacked
articles.summary: At least 23 protesters have been arrested in demonstrations in the capital.
articles.body:
Albanian riot police have fired tear gas and water cannons at hundreds of student demonstrators protesting over education and social conditions in the capital Tirana.

Protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at the Education Ministry on Tuesday, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

Student organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.

At least six officers and one female journalist were injured, according to a statement by police, and 23 people were arrested.

Police called on the protesters to stop attacking the ministry, but some attendees continued to assault officers with Molotov cocktails, firecrackers, stones and other hard objects, the statement said.

Protesters said they wanted to express frustration with inequality and government economic policies.

“What Albania needs is a revolution, a change, a complete overthrow of the system because it can’t go on like this,” protester Luljeta Kola said. She added that there was a deep social divide between the rich and the poor in the country.

Albania’s Deputy Prime Minister Albana Kociu wrote on Facebook: “Violence has not been, is not, and will never be a solution. Throwing stones, attacking institutions and the state police, as well as the senseless destruction of public property, are not how youth should express themselves.”

The Albanian capital has seen a series of anti-government protests since May , sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to US President Donald Trump’s family .

The project has fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency, with protesters demanding Rama’s resignation.

Students echoed those demands but told local media that Tuesday’s rally also aimed to decry university conditions, tuition fees and a lack of support for young people.

“Problems are not solved by pretending they do not exist. Students have questions, demands and plenty of reasons to be heard,” one of the organisers said on Instagram.

articles.title: INDIA bloc challenges SIR process but not its validity
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Why did opposition INDIA bloc, after making special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls the central point of its attack on Election
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Why did opposition INDIA bloc, after making special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls the central point of its attack on Election Commission and govt, give up the challenge to the constitutional and statutory validity of SIR in their joint writ petition before Supreme Court?Opposition members, led by LoP Rahul Gandhi, stated in the petition that they were not challenging SIR's validity in view of the SC judgement on Bihar SIR, which was conducted by EC based on its June 24, 2025, decision.That could be because SC in its May 27 judgement had examined the following questions - whether EC had the power to conduct SIR, whether SIR had a legitimate purpose and the process was proportionate to the object to be achieved, and whether the SIR procedure was contrary to Representation of the People Act and Registration of Electors Act, 1960 - and found there was nothing amiss in SIR's conduct or the process adopted to achieve the objective of weeding out voters who have died, shifted base or duplicate voters.SC had categorically ruled that SIR exercise "neither stands in direct conflict with RP Act and the 1960 Rules, nor does it detract from the constitutional imperative of free and fair elections".It had said, "The impugned SIR exercise, as conducted, satisfies requirements of proportionality. The measures adopted bear a rational nexus to the objective sought to be achieved, are not manifestly excessive, and are accompanied by sufficient procedural safeguards to prevent arbitrary exclusion."Since the judgement was of May 27, and attained finality as no one sought its review or correction, the INDIA bloc petitioners could not have challenged SIR's validity, thus limiting their challenge to alleged irregularities in the process of SIR and large-scale deletion of voters without giving them proper opportunity to rebut deletion.SC, in its five-month-old judgement, had said, "The statutory framework of RP Act itself provides for a situation where EC may direct a special revision under Section 21(3), in such manner as it may think fit and for reasons to be recorded."It also said "a reading of the impugned order, dated June 24, 2025, reveals EC has recorded the basis" on which it decided to conduct SIR. "We are equally satisfied that, in its object and design, the impugned SIR bears a direct nexus to the constitutional goal of a free and fair election. Free and fair elections do not rest merely upon the mechanics of polling. They equally depend upon the integrity, accuracy and purity of the electoral roll which forms the foundation of the democratic process," it had said."The impugned SIR, therefore, is not a process designed to subvert the established procedure, but one intended to secure the constitutional mandate of free and fair elections by ensuring the roll on which election rests is accurate and reliable," it had said, adding SIR had a direct nexus with the object of ensuring purity and accuracy of the electoral roll.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Sydney teen charged with murder of boy who was shot in face and neck
articles.summary: The 12-year-old was shot at a unit in Sydney last month and died in hospital three days later.
articles.body:
Australian police have charged a 19-year-old man with murder after a boy, aged 12, was fatally shot in the face and neck at a Sydney home last month.

Police were called to a unit in Sydney's northwest on 21 September after reports of a shooting. The boy was rushed to hospital in a critical condition and died three days later.

Nine people at the home when the shooting happened were uninjured. Three men - all aged 18 - were arrested with two later released without charge.

The third man, who has since turned 19, was initially charged with concealing a serious indictable offence and remanded in custody. On Tuesday, police charged him with murder. He is due to appear in court on Wednesday.

In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, New South Wales (NSW) police ruled out links to organised crime but days later, investigators said they were looking at possible gangland connections.

"A number of individuals that were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW Police and their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators," said Supt Naomi Moore last month.

Moore added that some of the people who were present at the time of the shooting were "not currently co-operating with investigators" and that police were yet to recover the firearm.

Local media reported that the incident was a suspected accident, citing police sources, and that the boy's father had paid tribute to his son on social media, posting a photo of the pair with the caption, "RIP my baby".

When the boy's death was announced, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said any incident "where we lose a young life in those circumstances is tragic".

articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday denied that Washington had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine and said he was working with both Kyiv and Moscow to end the Russia-Ukraine war.Addressing reporters before departing for a campaign in Alaska, Trump said both countries wanted the conflict to end but did not know how to reach that point."No, we haven't. So, we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end," Trump said.When asked what gave him confidence that Russian President Vladimir Putin wanted to end the war more than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump said his experience in negotiations informed his assessment."Only in dealing, that's what I've done my whole life is deals. articles.title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
articles.summary: AI dominates the translation business, but for high-stakes work, humans are still needed.
articles.body:
"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.

He thinks a new generation of tech will be an improvement.

"We will see translation systems that are increasingly capable of evaluating what they do and correcting themselves using different AI tools simultaneously: one to do the translation, a second to criticize it and a third to produce a new version, for example."

But perhaps the big moment will be when AI can show doubt.

"The real breakthrough won't come until these systems are not merely capable of translating but also of telling us when they're not sure," Yvon says.

articles.title: Winning entries for Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
articles.summary: Striking images including an urban coyote and an elephant carrying a dead calf are among this year's winners.
articles.body:
An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026.

While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed.

Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.

Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain.

Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females.

For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals."

He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said.

The competition's annual exhibition opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday 16 October 2026. Keep scrolling to see more award-winning images.

Category : Young Grand Title and 11 to 14 Years

Photographer : Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK

Location : Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe

Only by lying in the dust and capturing the beetle at eye level could Whitfield show how much strength its task required.

While on a family game drive in Zimbabwe, near his home in Victoria Falls, he spotted the dung beetle struggling to push a ball of dung uphill through the sand, with a trail of flies following closely behind. After experimenting with different angles and compositions, he captured a moment that reveals the extraordinary effort involved in this seemingly simple task.

articles.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write Caine Prize-winning story
articles.summary: Simbarashe Kundizeza was responding to an accusation that has caused an uproar on social media.
articles.body:
Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing.

His statement comes a week after he scooped the £10,000 ($13,000) award and a recent article in The Atlantic said AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.

"For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter," he posted on X .

The accusation has caused an uproar on social media and Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked that the US magazine had not waited for a full investigation before publishing.

"I do wish The Atlantic had spent more time investigating this so that alongside Pangram, they did have evidence of real human investigation of it before tainting the prize and tainting this winner," Wakatama told the BBC's Front Row programme .

The chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees said she had been contacted on Friday about the allegation and Vauhini Vara's article - Yet Another Prizewinner Seems to Be AI - had been published on Sunday.

It follows rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies .

Vara, who quoted Wakatama in her article, said her wariness of Silicon Valley was "well founded and reasonable" but she said Pangram's internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong.

The backlash to the article on social media has included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.

Wale Lawal, the Nigerian founder of The Republic magazine, called out The Atlantic article for being "crazy, racist and wildly unethical" .

Zimbabwean writer Joe Ruzvidzo, whose novel Welcome to Anywhere came out last year, said he stood by Kundizeza and that it was time "to fight this literary stop-and-frisk" .

Nigerian publisher Modupe Daramola said it was necessary to discuss how "these AI allegations are targeting Black and African writers" and how they were often disproportionately scrutinised.

"There's something incredibly sinister about this," the Noisy Streetss Limited publisher posted on X .

"Pangram is itself AI-powered. Why should its assessment be treated as definitive?" she added.

Wakatama said as part of an internal investigation for the Caine Prize Kundizeza would be sending in documentation about his various drafts and there were ongoing conversations with all the judges and The Shallow Tales Review, the publication that first published The Blue Fighter in 2025 .

In his statement, Kundizeza said had "a concrete, documented history" about the story's inspiration and he set out the chronology of its development.

Wakatama, who is also editor-at-large at Canongate Books, said Caine Prize submissions, which are all previously published, were not checked for AI, but writers vouched that their work was original.

She added that she was not against using AI per se to check entries, but she was "against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case".

Wakatama said it was also important to remember Pangram was "not yet tested".

"I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready."

Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated. Vara conceded that any AI-detection product, "including one as good of Pangram" was "not going to be 100% accurate".

In her article, as well as citing Pangram research she also quoted a recent paper by researchers at Free University of Brussels , which said it had found zero cases of Pangram, and two other AI-detection tools, getting it wrong when it came to English-language writing by non-native English speakers.

The study notes that tools like Pangram should be considered "as an initial flag for further investigation".

Vara told BBC's Front Row programme that she had also used her own judgment "to suss out these things" and that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".

"I also found an earlier 2021 story by the same author. I ran that through Pangram. It also came out as 100% human. And what struck me was that was a really good, interesting story. And tonally, it's so different from this story, as if the same person hadn't written both."

In response Kundizeza wrote: "To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing."

For Vara, one of the stylistic issues that stood out about The Blue Fighter was that it had used sentence constructions using "X but Y", which she says is common in AI-generated texts.

"Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come," is an example she gave from the story that described the character of the mother.

"The proliferation of those struck me," Vara told Front Row, adding that the story also had a lot of metaphors, also prevalent in writing generated by AI.

The day after winning the Caine Prize, Kundizeza told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.

He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.

"Much like the father in the story, my own dad... was an accountant, but he quit his job to grow tomatoes. So it kind of touches on both of our fathers," he told BBC Newsday.

On X, Kundizeza said he was heartened by "the numerous messages of solidarity from fellow writers and readers", ending his message by saying: "Most importantly, I will continue to write."

articles.title: Robot seized by German police after allegedly groping teenage girl
articles.summary: Police have launched an investigation on suspicion of sexual harassment after the robot's owner, 16, and his companion are said to have streamed the incident.
articles.body:
German police have launched an investigation into two teenagers accused of controlling a robot that allegedly groped a 16-year-old girl.

Police in Cologne have confiscated the red and gold robot that allegedly grabbed the girl's buttocks and made thrusting motions against her before she screamed and moved away.

North Rhine Westphalia Police said the robot's 16-year-old owner and his companion, 19, are believed to have streamed the incident live on social media and commented on it.

According to a police statement on Facebook, the 120cm (3.9ft) tall device approached the girl from behind while she was with her friends close to midnight local time (23:00 BST) on Saturday.

The girl was in front of a fast-food outlet near the city centre when the incident took place, police said.

Emergency services were alerted, and the teenage boy and the man now under investigation with him were found a block away a short time later. The robot was discovered in the back of a car, where the boy had placed it, police said.

A photo released by police showed the robot wearing a black moustache, a gold-coloured chain and white vest.

Along with the robot, police seized two mobile phones belonging to the suspects. They are trying to determine whether someone was deliberately controlling the robot's movements at the time of the incident.

In a follow-up post on Facebook, police warned some social media comments on the case "can be a crossing of the line and in the worst case, a criminal offense".

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV undergoes successful lung surgery after cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV under went successful surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung on Tuesday after an examination confirmed he had lung cancer.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV under went successful surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung on Tuesday after an examination confirmed he had lung cancer.Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected based on preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.“The operation was successful, and there were no complications,” the Holy See Press Office said.The Vatican said doctors were not currently considering chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of further tests. The Vatican press office noted that the medical statement's reference to the “radical” removal of the lobe indicated that doctors had removed all suspected tissue in the hope of eliminating any remaining traces of the cancer.The surgery took place at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and lasted around 90 minutes, according to the Holy See Press Office. The Pope spent approximately three hours in the operating room.Doctors used a video-assisted surgical technique to remove the affected portion of the lung. An examination of the tissue during the procedure confirmed the diagnosis, which had been suspected based on preoperative tests.Pope Leo awoke normally after the operation and returned to his room on the hospital's 10th floor following a brief period of observation, Vatican News reported.The surgical team was led by Professor Stefano Margaritora, assisted by Professor Elisa Meacci, Dr Maria Teresa Congedo and Dr Leonardo Petracca Ciavarella. Professor Massimo Antonelli, Dr Giovanni Punzo and Dr Giuseppe Bello were part of the anaesthesia team.Further tests on the removed tissue are expected in the coming days. Doctors had conducted preoperative examinations to establish the location of the affected tissue and plan the procedure.The Vatican has not announced any change to the Pope's expected hospital stay of one week.Following the surgery, Pope Leo asked for dinner and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff, Matteo Bruni, director of the Holy See Press Office, said, according to Vatican News.The Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic Hospital in Rome is a major medical centre that has treated several popes over the years.You use AI every day. articles.title: Murugan offers to resign, sparks Cab reshuffle buzz
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister L Murugan on Tuesday offered to resign from the Cabinet and Rajya Sabha, saying he wanted to return to politics in his home
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister L Murugan on Tuesday offered to resign from the Cabinet and Rajya Sabha, saying he wanted to return to politics in his home state, Tamil Nadu, after being part of govt for over five years. This rekindled the buzz that PM Modi could be preparing to reshuffle his council of ministers amid a steady exit of its members and some being in the queue.Murugan has three and a half years left of his RS term, and his exit will allow BJP to pick a new face from Madhya Pradesh, where he was elected from in 2024.In his five-page letter, Murugan expressed gratitude to the PM for all the opportunities he got and his govt's work for Tamil Nadu. He said, "I therefore request you to relieve me of my responsibilities as Minister of State and permit me to relinquish my membership of the Rajya Sabha so that I may dedicate myself full-time to strengthening the party in Tamil Nadu."What stoked curiosity in political circles is that he chose to post the letter offering his resignation on social media, apparently with the consent of the BJP leadership. This suggested a clear signal from the party brass, leaving many within the governing alliance wondering if it was a prelude to more resignations.Rajya Sabha vacancy may open up possibilities for PuriL Murugan's exit comes on heels of BJP not renominating ministers Hardeep Puri and B L Verma for another term in RS. Ravneet Bittu and George Kurian have already resigned earlier under similar circumstances.Two other ministers, Pankaj Chaudhary and Harsh Malhotra, have been made chiefs of BJP units in UP and Delhi, making their departure only a matter of time.Interestingly, an imminent RS vacancy from MP opens up the possibility for Puri, the lone Sikh face in the govt, to return to Rajya Sabha.Murugan has been BJP chief in Tamil Nadu, the last one among big states where BJP remains on the margins of electoral politics, and it was given a jolt when K Annamalai, who enjoyed a decent following, quit in June 2026.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Online influencer Clavicular is facing a criminal case in Massachusetts after allegations involving a 2025 encounter, but a related civil lawsuit has
articles.body: Online influencer Clavicular is facing a criminal case in Massachusetts after allegations involving a 2025 encounter, but a related civil lawsuit has taken a new turn. The woman who accused him of sexual assault has removed those claims from her latest court filing. Her attorney says the decision aims to prevent the civil proceedings from interfering with the criminal prosecution. However, the lawsuit continues over separate allegations involving cosmetic injections, alleged deception and emotional distress.Clavicular's accuser withdraws sexual assault claims from civil lawsuitAleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, an 18-year-old influencer known online as Alorah or Alorah Ziva, filed an amended complaint in Miami-Dade County, Florida, removing the sexual assault allegations against Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular.According to NBC News, Mendoza's attorney, Drew Moss, said the decision was linked to the pending criminal case in Massachusetts. The change does not mean the criminal allegations have been dismissed. Peters, 20, was charged in September with rape, drugging someone for sexual intercourse and procuring liquor for a person under 21. He has denied the allegations.The criminal complaint concerns an alleged incident at Peters' family's home on Cape Cod in May 2025. Mendoza alleged that Peters arranged an Uber for her, gave her vodka and sexually assaulted her. The original civil complaint also alleged that he had sex with her when she was too intoxicated to consent and while she was asleep.The amended filing uses different language, stating that Peters "had sex with Mendoza multiple times while she was intoxicated." It no longer includes the earlier explicit allegations of nonconsensual sex.Moss explained the decision in a statement to NBC News.“In light of Mr. Peters’ recent posts and other conduct, this matter is more appropriate for the criminal justice system,” Mendoza’s lawyer, Drew Moss, said in a statement, noting that the sexual assault claim was dropped “due to the pending criminal charges in Massachusetts.” “Ms. Mendoza does not want her civil case to interfere with that process.”Peters has previously denied the criminal allegations. His spokesperson declined to comment on the latest civil complaint.Clavicular still faces claims over alleged cosmetic injectionsAlthough Mendoza has removed the sexual assault claims from her civil lawsuit, several other allegations remain. The amended complaint accuses Peters of battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, fraudulent misrepresentation, fraudulent concealment and unauthorised publication of name and likeness.The dispute also involves an alleged incident during a November 2025 livestream in Florida. Mendoza claims Peters injected her face with Aqualyx, a fat-dissolving compound, without her consent. She alleges that he did not disclose that the substance was not approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and misled her about what he was injecting.The filing further alleges that Peters knew Mendoza was 17 at the time. It includes screenshots of livestream comments in which viewers allegedly warned him about her age.The criminal proceedings in Massachusetts remain separate from the civil case in Florida. Peters' next scheduled hearing appeared on the court docket as October 22, after his previously planned October 14 arraignment was cancelled.For now, the amended complaint narrows the civil dispute without resolving the outstanding allegations. The criminal case will proceed through the Massachusetts justice system, where the charges must be addressed through the legal process.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Texas DA says ICE intentionally hit immigrant with a car and may have withheld evidence
articles.summary: Harris County DA Sean Teare told NBC News his office has collected multiple videos for its own investigation but isn’t getting cooperation from the federal government.
articles.body: HOUSTON — Videos collected by local investigators make it “pretty obvious” that an ICE officer intentionally ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez during an immigration stop Saturday, which could lead to assault charges, the district attorney said Tuesday. “This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News. Teare said the federal government is not cooperating with the investigation conducted by his office and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. He also said ICE may have allowed the erasure of critical data in the vehicle involved in striking Parra, who was on foot. Teare said that in his seven years as a Harris County vehicular crimes division chief, he has reviewed video from a number of other auto-pedestrian collision cases. He said the video his investigators have gathered in Parra’s case “goes above” the video that was posted online and obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston. “My viewing of it, and many other investigators that have viewed it, as well, it’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said. Parra, 48, was left with multiple breaks and fractures in his body, according to his attorney and an advocate who has been speaking on his behalf. He had surgery on one leg and faces multiple additional operations, said Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL, an immigrant civil rights group. Video obtained by KPRC shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. It shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running. It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows. An ICE spokesman said over the weekend that officers were pursuing the fleeing men and that “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.” Teare, a Democrat, announced late Monday that his office had launched an independent investigation. On Tuesday, an ICE spokesperson who was not identified said in a statement that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.” ICE said the allegations are “disgusting smears” that are “peddled by the media,” leading to more than a 1,600% increase in assaults and a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against its law enforcement officers. It did not offer data behind those numbers. ICE has said that Parra was not the target of the attempted stop but that he was in the country illegally. Parra’s attorney and family have said he has no criminal record and was on his way to work applying stucco. Teare said his office and the sheriff’s office determined that the vehicle that struck Parra was a Jeep Cherokee and that it potentially had evidence, including a data crash recorder. He said his office wanted to know whether the vehicle locked in information at the time of the collision that could be downloaded, such as speed, steering and braking. Teare said the way to preserve data from the car would have been to “put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.” But he said he believes any data on the recorder related to the incident could have been erased when ICE drove the car away. He and the sheriff’s investigators told ICE the information needed to be downloaded, but ICE refused, Teare said. ICE did not respond to questions about a data crash recorder, the erasing of any potential data or any refusal to download it. “Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that.” Teare also said two people from “an entirely different operation” were in the back seat of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Those two people are also in ICE custody, along with Parra. Teare said his office is working to ensure all three remain in the country as material witnesses. “I’ve taught for years at the Houston Police Department Academy, Harris County Department Academy. I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the United States that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” he said. Doing so puts “every single person out there in danger again,” he said. According to Teare, the ICE vehicle should have activated its emergency equipment, such as its lights and siren, as it jumped a median and crossed into oncoming traffic. A senior official at the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News on Tuesday that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras. ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation, the official said. Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear whether there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows. ICE has said it was targeting another man, Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. Espinoza and Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said neither Parra nor the man who was with him when ICE stopped their vehicle has any association with Mendoza. In previous encounters between ICE and targets of its arrests in vehicle stops, including some who have been killed, such as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, ICE has alleged the people it tried to arrest weaponized their vehicles. Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops. The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras. The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has been asking witnesses and people who may have photos or video of the incident to contact it. Teare said that there is a secure portal that goes directly to the district attorney’s office and that no one is asked about citizenship or immigration status. “All we are interested in is getting the truth, and any shred of cellphone footage, anyone that saw something and really can point us in the right direction, it would be wonderful,” he said.

articles.title: A couple bought a 3.04-hectare Australian estate for A$1.6 million and restored a derelict 1932 woodcutter’s cabin; the two-bedroom retreat now earns up to A$50,000 a year as a holiday rental
articles.summary: A neglected timber cabin tucked inside a rainforest estate on Queensland’s Gold Coast has become a source of rental income after its owners restored the
articles.body: A neglected timber cabin tucked inside a rainforest estate on Queensland’s Gold Coast has become a source of rental income after its owners restored the historic structure into a two-bedroom holiday retreat. The property, located in Bonogin, is now heading to auction, with its unusual combination of contemporary architecture, equestrian facilities and a heritage cottage drawing attention in the local property market. The story was reported by The Gold Coast Bulletin, with property details also listed by realestate (dot) com (dot) au and other Australian property portals. Marlon Sayer and Romolo Romeo purchased the 3.04-hectare estate at 14 Fowler Court in 2016 for A$1.6 million. While the main residence was designed by architect Michael Witty and built in 2007, the property also contained a much older structure that had fallen into disrepair.A forgotten cabin with a century of historyThe timber cabin dates to 1932 and is associated with the region’s early timber-cutting history. Research by the owners linked it to Frederick Fowler, a pioneering timber hauler whose name was later given to the street. When the couple first inspected the property, the cabin was in poor condition, with visible mould and signs of neglect. Rather than demolish it, they decided to restore the building and preserve its distinctive character.From dilapidated shack to rainforest retreatThe renovation retained several original features, including the cedar exterior, slate flooring and A-frame roof. Exposed beams and the cottage’s rustic character were also preserved, while substantial improvements made it suitable for modern guests. The owners installed a new kitchen, added a bathroom and repaired the structure’s essential services. The fireplace was refreshed with individually painted bricks, and a deck was added to extend the living space into the surrounding rainforest.The finished cabin has two loft-style bedrooms beneath its pitched roof, alongside an open-plan living and dining area. Its secluded setting and outdoor deck give the property a different character from the larger, contemporary home elsewhere on the estate. The restoration has also given the old building a new commercial purpose. Operating as a holiday rental, the cabin reportedly charges about A$300 a night and generates between A$45,000 and A$50,000 annually, according to the Gold Coast Bulletin report. Actual earnings can vary depending on occupancy, seasonal demand and running costs.A luxury estate with a distinctive mix of featuresThe cabin is only one part of the property being marketed as Pegasus. The main house has four bedrooms and features soaring ceilings, New Guinea rosewood finishes and a subterranean wine cellar designed to accommodate approximately 600 bottles. Outdoor amenities include a 120,000-litre swimming pool, an entertaining terrace with an outdoor kitchen and views across the surrounding valley. The grounds also include rainforest areas, a freshwater creek and walking trails.For buyers interested in keeping horses, the estate has relatively level paddocks, stables, a tack room, a washing bay and a dam. The rental income from the cabin has helped the owners offset the expenses associated with maintaining the horses, according to the report. The property’s appeal lies in the contrast between the architect-designed residence and the modest timber cottage, which offers a separate accommodation option without losing its historic identity.Property goes to auctionAfter a decade at the estate, the retired owners are preparing to downsize. Realestate (dot) com (dot) au listing confirms that the property is scheduled to go to auction on October 30, 2026, with Hayley Kidson and Marco De Vincentiis of Kollosche handling the sale.The property is being marketed without a disclosed asking price. Its eventual sale will determine how buyers value the combination of the main residence, extensive grounds, equestrian facilities and income-producing cabin. The restored cottage offers a reminder that older structures on large properties can have value beyond their original purpose. In Bonogin, a building that was once close to being overlooked has become a working holiday retreat, adding another dimension to an estate defined by both modern design and local history.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: How to grow curry leaves in a pot and 7 mistakes that can kill the plant
articles.summary: Growing any type of plant in a pot at home can be challenging.
articles.body: Growing any type of plant in a pot at home can be challenging. However, when it comes to Curry leaves, the benefits and convenience of having them at home make it a practical choice. Freshly grown leaves can instantly provide an aromatic and citrusy fresh flavour to your cooking that store-bought leaves cannot match. With multiple hair and skin benefits also associated with them, curry leaves make for a great plant to grow at home.Growing curry leaves in a potted plant begins with ensuring the environment is correct. Curry leaves don’t grow the same in each season and can require different care depending on the moisture in the air. With first selecting a pot at least 12 inches in height, either made of clay or terracotta, the next step is to prepare the soil. A combination of garden soil, cow manure, vermicompost, compost or coco peat can be used in equal parts. After preparing the right soil, the plant requires a minimum of six hours of sunlight daily and an adequate amount of water, which can vary depending upon the season.A new curry leaves sapling needs time and attention; its root system takes nearly a year to mature before the leaves can be fully grown or used. The challenge in growing curry leaves at home, however, can begin with common mistakes that can actually kill the plant even before it reaches full growth.Soil preparationThe soil is the heart of any root system; if it lacks quality or the right proportions, it can affect the roots and prevent them from receiving the nutrients needed for the plant to survive. Moreover, using fresh or uncomposted manure risks burning the plant's roots by introducing harmful pathogens.Plant wateringBoth over-watering and inadequate watering can cause the root system to not receive the right amount of moisture, sending the plant into extreme stress. Watering habits in summers might mean watering once every day, and in springtime, once or twice a week.Not picking the right potThe height of the potted plant is perhaps the most important step when beginning to grow curry leaves and a common mistake people make. A tall terracotta pot allows for easier water drainage. If a small pot is picked, water from the soil will have to be drained into a larger container, as improper drainage or the absence of drainage holes limits the oxygen required for the roots to grow.Improper root growthIf the roots in the pot do not receive enough space to grow, they can circle around the pot tightly. In this case, repotting becomes essential, as the roots need space to grow and breathe.Not providing enough sunlightSunlight, crucial for the plant’s photosynthesis process, is a key requirement, with 6 to 8 hours of sunlight recommended for the curry leaves pot. This ensures that the plant, in a lack of sunlight, does not develop chlorosis, where the yellowing of the leaves and the appearance of dark spots can slowly weaken the plant.Over-pruningWhile pruning can help the curry leaves plant grow bushier, excessive pruning can put unnecessary stress on a young plant. If you prune too many leaves or branches at once, the plant will have fewer leaves to support its growth. So prune gradually and give the plant time to recover and produce new growth.Ignoring pestsPests can become another common problem when growing curry leaves at home, particularly when the plant is kept in a warm environment. Small insects can settle on the leaves and stems, slowly affecting the plant’s health and new growth. Ignoring these signs for too long can allow the infestation to spread, weakening the plant before the problem is noticed.For a bushy curry leaves pot, patience goes a long way. Growing curry leaves and waiting before using them can be a long process, however, the benefits of this rich and incredibly beneficial plant can only be reaped with due patience, time and by avoiding common mistakes that can hamper its growth.You use AI every day. articles.title: Reparations official demands compensation beyond a 'single check' as advocates make progress in California
articles.summary: California's Truth in Disclosure Act is now law, but reparations advocates say corporate transparency is just the beginning of a larger fight.
articles.body: Advocates for racial reparations celebrated a legislative victory in California after Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2599 — the Truth in Disclosure Act — into law. But key figures behind the effort say corporate transparency is only a starting point, maintaining that direct cash compensation remains essential. Kristin Nimmers, policy and campaign manager for the California Black Power Network (CBPN) and the Alliance for Reparations, Reconciliation, and Truth, told Fox News Digital financial reparations must go far beyond a "single check." "We really focus on a harm-based approach, so whoever was harmed should be entitled to that repair," Nimmers said. "Compensation for slavery, unpaid labor, for the 40 acres and a mule that were promised after the end of slavery — that should go to folks who have lineage and are descendants of people who were enslaved because that is the harm that is being repaired." REPARATIONS ADVOCATES SLAM CASH COMPENSATION ‘HANDOUT’ LABEL, POINT TO PAST GOVERNMENT REMEDIES However, Nimmers emphasized that racial inequities persisted long after the end of chattel slavery. "Black Americans were denied wages. We were denied property. We were denied access to capital. We were denied access to equal education — all of that over hundreds of years," Nimmers added. "And, so, a single check is not going to holistically repair our communities." AB 2599 requires qualifying corporations doing business in California with more than $100 million in gross revenue to search their historical records and publicly disclose any financial ties to chattel slavery. Lawmakers and advocacy groups are now attempting to leverage the bill's passage as momentum to turn broader recommendations from the California Reparations Task Force into law. During the multiyear tenure of the California Task Force to Study and Develop Reparation Proposals for African Americans (established under AB 3121), CBPN served as an official state community anchor. The coalition facilitated grassroots civic engagement across California, hosting listening sessions to gather public testimony that directly informed the task force’s landmark 1,100-page final report issued in 2023. CALIFORNIA COUNTY APPROVES REPARATIONS PLAN AS NEIGHBORING SCHOOL DISTRICT 'BLACK THRIVING' EFFORT STALLS However, the path forward for direct cash payouts remains difficult. While Newsom signed AB 2599, the governor has consistently taken a cautious stance on direct financial restitution, resisting high-cost payout proposals and vetoing related financial measures backed by progressive lawmakers. Newsom's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment regarding CBPN's support for cash payments. Progressive coalitions also face internal ideological divisions within the broader movement. Grassroots organizations like the U.S. Freedmen Project, comprised of self-identified "Foundational Black Americans," strongly disagree with broader, harm-based eligibility frameworks. The group aims to educate the public on the legal and historical distinctions between African Americans who directly descend from enslaved people in the U.S. and those who voluntarily immigrated to the country in recent decades. The U.S. Freedmen Project told Fox News Digital that recent immigrants and Black Americans who do not meet its ancestry criteria should not be included in government reparations programs, arguing that left-leaning advocates are using the legacy of slavery to fund a far broader social platform. Nimmers pushed back on lineage-only requirements, arguing that systemic discrimination in the 20th century affected a wider range of Black residents. NEWSOM SIGNS FIRST-IN-NATION LAW FORCING MAJOR COMPANIES TO REVEAL SLAVERY-ERA TIES: 'MAKE IT PUBLIC' "If you are a Black person — maybe a Black immigrant who came here in the 1950s before the Civil Rights Act was passed — then you also experienced segregated schools," Nimmers said. "If you experienced segregated schools, if you experienced redlining, and we are coming up with some sort of policy or some sort of form of repair for those things, then you should also be included in the group that is repaired. It isn’t really a lineage-based outlook but more of a harm-based approach." While state-level cash proposals remain stalled, localized initiatives have moved forward. Earlier this year, the Reparations Committee in Evanston, Illinois, approved $25,000 housing grants to 44 Black residents. City officials focused on housing, calling historical redlining and discriminatory zoning "the strongest case for reparations." For California advocates, the long-term goal remains a comprehensive package encompassing both financial compensation and systemic policy reform. "What is the repair for that harm, and who fits within the group that was harmed? It's necessary because we are owed that compensation for unpaid labor and historical harms."

articles.title: Rajnath, Czech first deputy PM agree to expand defence cooperation between two countries
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Tuesday held a bilateral meeting with First Deputy PM and minister of industry and trade of Czech Republic
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Tuesday held a bilateral meeting with First Deputy PM and minister of industry and trade of Czech Republic Karel Havlícek and agreed to further expand defence cooperation as both reviewed the entire spectrum of defence industrial cooperation between the two countries.While the two sides welcomed the ongoing collaboration and successful establishment of various joint ventures, they agreed to expand this cooperation, including under the aegis of India-Czech Joint Defence Committee to promote ‘Make-in-India’ and ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’. The two also discussed the ongoing issues of peace and security and acknowledged the need for greater cooperation to maintain regional stability. They reiterated that the partnership between India and Czech Republic is based on historical and cultural ties, and shared values of mutual trust and respect.Havlícek, who is on a four-day visit to India and is interacting with various ministries, trade and businesses, is scheduled to visit Mumbai and Bengaluru.Defence secretary in Cyprus to boost security cooperationDefence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh met Chief of the National Guard of the Republic of Cyprus Lt Gen Emmanouel Theodorou to discuss bilateral defence and security cooperation and regional security developments. Both sides agreed to enhance military-to-military engagement and explore collaboration in training and capacity building in emerging domains, including AI, cyber security, electronic warfare and multi-domain operations. After visiting Cyprus, the defence secretary will tour Greece to boost maritime security and defence industrial cooperation

articles.title: Attorney says fatal Six Flags roller coaster accident could raise broader safety questions as 9 rides close
articles.summary: A personal injury attorney outlines potential liability as investigators examine the fatal roller coaster accident at Six Flags Over Georgia.
articles.body: A fatal roller coaster incident at Six Flags Over Georgia is raising questions about ride safety and potential liability as investigators work to determine how a rider was ejected from one of the park's attractions. The man was killed Monday while riding Goliath, the tallest roller coaster at the park, which features a 200-foot first hill. Police and state ride inspectors are investigating, while Six Flags temporarily closed nine similar roller coasters across North America following the death, according to The Associated Press. Mark Lopez-Trigo, a Florida personal injury attorney and founding partner of Padron & Lopez-Trigo, told Fox News Digital that investigators will likely examine whether the incident was isolated or points to an issue with the ride's safety equipment, maintenance or inspections. "What led to this incident, whether it be isolated or system-wide?" Lopez-Trigo said. "Was it a failure in the system itself?" MAN DIES AFTER FALLING FROM GOLIATH ROLLER COASTER AT SIX FLAGS OVER GEORGIA Investigators could examine Goliath's restraint system and whether required maintenance and inspections were properly conducted leading up to the incident, he said. "All that's going to hopefully come out in the next couple days throughout the investigation," he said. Lopez-Trigo stressed that the investigation remains in its early stages and that the cause has not been determined. Six Flags' decision to temporarily close similar rides could help narrow the investigation, Lopez-Trigo said, though the closures alone do not establish a broader safety problem. "It tells us where to focus theories of liability," he said. Goliath does not take riders upside down and uses lap bars that pull down over riders' legs and waists rather than seat belts, according to The Associated Press. Lopez-Trigo said cases involving alleged safety-equipment failures often require investigators and attorneys to look beyond the moments immediately preceding an accident. MAN'S FATAL FALL FROM SIX FLAGS ROLLER COASTER SPARKS HORRIFYING EYEWITNESS ACCOUNTS "Usually what it boils down to is, like what I said, some sort of trickle down effect where a certain system either wasn't maintained properly or wasn't inspected properly," he said, speaking generally about cases his firm has handled. For the victim's family, potential civil litigation could include a wrongful-death claim brought through the victim's estate, while injured guests could have separate personal injury claims, depending on the circumstances, Lopez-Trigo said. While those claims involve different legal rights and damages, he said the process of determining what happened and who, if anyone, bears responsibility would likely be similar. "While justice might mean different things to the different parties, the path to getting that justice is probably gonna look similar in terms of finding some of the answers as to how this happened," he said. Lopez-Trigo said the closure of nine similar coasters underscores how much remains unknown. "Six Flags' decision to temporarily close nine other roller coasters across six parks tells you that the company itself does not yet know what caused this," he said. WOMAN ALLEGEDLY EJECTED FROM ROLLER COASTER, SUFFERS SERIOUS INJURIES AFTER DRAGGED ALONG TRACK: REPORTS Determining the cause will be critical not only to potential civil claims but also to identifying whether safety changes are needed, Lopez-Trigo said. "When we've dealt with cases like this in the past, it was always extremely important to find out what happened," he said, adding that uncovering the facts can help prevent similar incidents.
